title: Cercopes
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 8719b7d375018d4f. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: The Trojan ships row clear of Charybdis and, with the Ausonian shore already close at hand, are blown back to the coast of Libya, where the woman of Sidon takes Aeneas into her heart and her house and then, unable to bear his going, falls on a blade on a pyre built under the pretence of a rite. Carried back a second time to the ground of Eryx and to faithful Acestes, he sacrifices and honours his own father's tomb, then puts to sea again past the kingdom of Hippotes' son, lands smoking with hot sulphur and the Sirens' crags, to Inarime, Prochyte and Pithecusae. That last island is named after the people who once lived there: the Cercopes, whom the father of the gods, sick of their cheating and their false oaths, shrank into apes and left able to do nothing but screech.

sentences.t:
Hunc ubi Troianae remis avidamque Charybdim
evicere rates, cum iam prope litus adesset
Ausonium, Libycas vento referuntur ad oras.
sentences.l: When the Trojan ships had overcome this one and greedy Charybdis with their oars, though the Ausonian shore was already near at hand, they are carried back by the wind to Libyan coasts.
sentences.i: When the Trojan ships had pulled clear of that one and of ravenous Charybdis, with the shore of Ausonia already close at hand, the wind carried them back to the coast of Libya.
sentences.n: Ubi with the perfect is “when” of a completed action, and evicere is the poetic third-person plural perfect, the short form of evicerunt; -ere for -erunt is the regular verse alternative and worth learning on sight. After ubi English wants a pluperfect, “had overcome”. Hunc is masculine accusative singular and its antecedent stands in the lines before this part, so nothing here can fix it; what these lines do show is that it is joined by -que to avidam Charybdim and that the two are overcome together. Remis is an ablative of means, “with the oars”: the sea-room is won by rowing. Cum with the imperfect subjunctive adesset is the circumstantial cum, and the sense here is nearly concessive — the coast was in reach and they lost it — which the literal brings out with “though”. Magnus prints adesset, whose subject is litus ... Ausonium, “the Ausonian shore was near”; some editions print adessent, which makes the ships the subject and prope litus Ausonium the place they had almost reached. Litus stands in 76 and its adjective Ausonium at the head of 77, split across the line-end by adesset, so Italy is named a line late. Referuntur is present and passive, “they are carried back”, after the perfect evicere: the narrative slips into the present at the moment the wind takes charge, and the passive leaves the ships nothing to do.

sentences.l: There the Sidonian woman receives Aeneas both in heart and in house, she who was to bear not well the parting from her Phrygian husband;
sentences.i: There the woman of Sidon takes Aeneas in, into her heart and into her house — she who was to take the parting from her Phrygian husband very hard indeed;
sentences.n: Excipit stands first and is a historic present, “receives”, although the events are long past. Animoque domoque is the doubled -que ... -que, “both ... and”, two ablatives under one verb, one of them a feeling and one of them a building, so a single act of taking him in is at once private and public. Latura is the future active participle of fero, the form that says what someone is going to do or is fated to do; non bene latura, “going to bear it not well”, is litotes, an understatement that means the opposite of mild, and the line and a half that follows shows how far it understates. Discidium is the word for the breaking off of a marriage, and mariti is an objective genitive after it — the separation from her husband. Phrygius means Trojan. The subject is held back to the head of 80, the third line of the sentence: Sidonis, a Greek-style feminine noun, “the woman of Sidon”, Sidon being a Phoenician city. She is named by her city and not by her name; the queen meant is Dido. Maritus, “husband”, is the poem's own word for what Aeneas is to her.

sentences.t:
inque pyra sacri sub imagine facta
incubuit ferro deceptaque decipit omnes.
sentences.l: and on a pyre built under the appearance of a rite she fell upon the blade, and, deceived, she deceives everyone.
sentences.i: and on a pyre raised under the show of a sacred rite she fell on the sword — herself cheated, she cheats them all.
sentences.n: Inque is et in, with the -que hung on the preposition but joining the whole clause. Pyra ... facta is the ablative after in, facta being the perfect passive participle, “made, built”. Sacri is the neuter noun sacrum, “a rite, a sacrifice”, in the genitive after sub imagine: imago here is not a picture but a semblance, a front, so the pyre was passed off as an altar. Incubuit governs the dative ferro — incumbere with the dative is the standing Latin for lying down upon a thing — and ferrum, “the iron”, is the ordinary metonymy for a blade. Deceptaque decipit is polyptoton, the same verb turned twice: the perfect passive participle, “having been deceived”, against the present active, “she deceives”. Who deceived her these lines do not say; what she deceives everyone about is the pyre. The tense turns as well, from the perfect incubuit to the present decipit, so the deceiving outlasts the act that ends her.

sentences.l: Again, fleeing the new walls of the sandy land, and carried back to the seats of Eryx and to faithful Acestes, he sacrifices and honours the mound of his own father;
sentences.i: Fleeing once more the new walls of that sandy country, and brought back to the ground of Eryx and to loyal Acestes, he offers sacrifice and pays honour at his own father's tomb;
sentences.n: The subject is not named. Aeneas was the accusative object Aenean at 78, and here he becomes the subject of sacrificat and honorat without being renamed — Latin can carry a person that far on the verb ending alone. Rursus, “again”, opens 82, and relatus is the perfect passive participle of refero, the same verb that carried the ships to Africa at 77 with referuntur: he is carried back a second time, in the other direction. Harenosae ... terrae is a genitive with moenia, “the walls of the sandy land”, the African coast of 77; nova says the walls are newly built, and the city goes unnamed. Ad governs both sedes and Acesten, one preposition over two objects joined by -que, and Acesten is a Greek accusative. Sui genitoris is the reflexive, “of his own father”, though the sentence names no subject for it to reflect. Tumulus is the raised mound heaped over a grave, so the honour is paid at a place, not to a person. Magnus prints ad sedes; some editions print ad sedemque, singular and with a second connective, giving “to both the seat of Eryx and faithful Acestes”.

sentences.t:
quasque rates Iris Iunonia paene cremarat,
solvit et Hippotadae regnum terrasque calenti
sulphure fumantes Acheloiadumque relinquit
Sirenum scopulos,
sentences.l: And the ships which Junonian Iris had almost burned he casts off, and he leaves behind the kingdom of the son of Hippotes, and lands smoking with hot sulphur, and the crags of the Sirens, daughters of Achelous,
sentences.i: And the ships that Juno's Iris had all but burned he unmoors, and leaves astern the realm of Hippotes' son, and the lands that smoke with hot sulphur, and the crags of the Sirens, the daughters of Achelous,
sentences.n: Quasque is a connecting relative, quas with -que, opening the clause: English wants “and the ships which”, not a bare relative. The antecedent rates is drawn inside the relative clause, so quas rates is the object of cremarat and the main verb solvit takes the same ships as its object without naming them again. Cremarat is syncopated cremaverat, a pluperfect — the near-burning is older than everything else here. Iunonia makes Iris Juno's; the adjective does the work an English possessive would. Solvit is spelt alike in the present and in the perfect and cannot be told apart here, and the presents around it, relinquit and legit, make the present the likelier reading; solvere of a ship is to cast off, to loose the moorings. Hippotadae is a Greek patronymic in the genitive, “of the son of Hippotes”, meaning Aeolus, who keeps the winds. Terras ... fumantes takes the ablative of means calenti sulphure, “smoking with hot sulphur” — volcanic ground, named by its smell rather than by a name. Acheloiadum is a Greek genitive plural, “of the daughters of Achelous”, and it is cut off from the noun-group Sirenum scopulos by the verb relinquit and by the line-end between 87 and 88, so the rocks themselves arrive last of all.

sentences.t:
orbataque praeside pinus
Inarimen Prochytenque legit sterilique locatas
colle Pithecusas, habitantum nomine dictas.
sentences.l: and the pine, robbed of its protector, skirts Inarime and Prochyte and Pithecusae, set on a barren hill, called by the name of their inhabitants.
sentences.i: and the ship, robbed of the one who watched over it, coasts along Inarime and Prochyte and Pithecusae, perched on its barren hill and called after the name of those who lived there.
sentences.n: Pinus is a pine tree standing for the ship built out of it, the material named for the thing. Orbata is the participle of orbare, to bereave, with praeside as an ablative of separation: robbed of its praeses, its guard or protector. Who that was these lines do not say. Legere of a coast is to pick one's way along it: the verb is the ordinary lego, “gather, pick”, used of hugging a shoreline. Inarimen and Prochyten are Greek accusatives. Sterili is parted from its noun colle by locatas and by the line-end between 89 and 90, so the barrenness is felt before the hill it belongs to; locatas, “placed, set”, agrees with Pithecusas. Habitantum is the genitive plural of the present participle habitans in its shorter poetic form, for habitantium: “of the dwellers”. Pithecusae is a Greek name built on pithekos, “ape”, so habitantum nomine dictas, “called by the name of the inhabitants”, is an etymology laid down as a plain fact — and the next line begins the story that has to explain it.

sentences.t:
Quippe deum genitor, fraudem et periuria quondam
Cercopum exosus gentisque admissa dolosae,
in deforme viros animal mutavit,
sentences.l: For indeed the father of the gods, having come to hate the fraud and the perjuries of the Cercopes long before, and the deeds committed by that guileful race, changed the men into a misshapen animal,
sentences.i: For the father of the gods, sick long since of the Cercopes' cheating and their false oaths, and of what that guileful people had done, turned the men into a misshapen animal,
sentences.n: Quippe, “for indeed”, marks what follows as the explanation of the name just given: the whole story is an aetiology hung on an island. Deum is the shortened genitive plural for deorum, and genitor is “begetter”, so the father of the gods is named by title and not by name. Exosus is passive in form but active in meaning — it takes the accusative objects fraudem, periuria and admissa — and means “having come to hate”, which English has to render actively. Admissa is the neuter plural participle used as a noun, “things let in”, hence “things committed”, offences; the genitive that owns them, gentis ... dolosae, is split around it. Fraus, periurium and dolosus are the poem's own words for these people: cheating, false oaths, guile, and the punishment is announced as deserved before it is described. In with the accusative after mutavit is the regular way of naming what a thing is turned into. Deforme and animal stand on either side of viros, so the men are shut inside the beast in the word order of 93 before they are shut inside it in the story.

sentences.t:
ut idem
dissimiles homini possent similesque videri,
sentences.l: so that the same ones could be seen to be unlike a man and like him,
sentences.i: so that the same creatures could look both unlike a man and like one,
sentences.n: Ut with the imperfect subjunctive possent depends on mutavit, and these lines do not decide which of two readings it carries: purpose, “so that they might be able to seem”, which makes the paradox the design of Jupiter, or result, “with the effect that they could seem”, which makes it what the change produced. There is no correlative word in the main clause to settle it and no negative to test it with, so the literal keeps the neutral “so that ... could”. Idem here is the masculine nominative plural, the contracted form of eidem — the same beings, before the change and after it — and not the neuter singular it looks like. Dissimiles opens 94 and similesque follows possent, so the two adjectives sit on either side of the verb; one dative, homini, serves both, since similis and dissimilis take the dative of the thing likened. Videri is the passive infinitive of video, “to be seen”, which Latin uses where English says “seem”, and the passive matters: the paradox is about how the creatures look to someone else. That paradox is the point the aetiology has been building towards — an ape is a man's likeness and his unlikeness in one body.

sentences.t:
membraque contraxit naresque a fronte resimas
contudit et rugis peraravit anilibus ora
totaque velatos flaventi corpora villo
misit in has sedes
sentences.l: and he drew their limbs together, and pounded flat their nostrils, snubbed back from the brow, and furrowed their faces right across with an old woman's wrinkles, and sent them, veiled as to their whole bodies with tawny shag, into these dwellings
sentences.i: and he shrank their limbs; he beat their nostrils flat, snubbed up from the brow; he ploughed their faces over with the wrinkles of an old woman; and with their whole bodies shrouded in tawny fur he sent them off to these dwellings
sentences.n: Four verbs in four lines, strung on -que, -que, et and -que, and every one of them a physical act done to a body: contraxit, drew together; contudit, pounded; peraravit, ploughed through; misit, sent. Resimas is the adjective for a nose bent back and turned up, and a fronte, “from the brow”, traces the line it follows down the face. Peraravit is per with arare, to plough, so the furrows are drawn right across, and the wrinkles are anilibus, “of an old woman” — a judgement rather than a measurement. Totaque ... corpora is an accusative standing beside the passive participle velatos, and it can be taken two ways: as the Greek accusative of respect, “veiled as to their whole bodies”, or as the participle used in a middle sense with a direct object, “having veiled their whole bodies”. The two come to the same English, and a passive participle with a bare accusative beside it is a shape worth recognising on sight. Villus is the shaggy coat of an animal and not human hair; flaventi is “turning yellow”, tawny. Has sedes, “these dwellings”, points back at the islands named at 89 and 90.

sentences.t:
nec non prius abstulit usum
verborum et natae dira in periuria linguae:
sentences.l: and moreover he took away beforehand the use of words and of a tongue born for dreadful perjuries:
sentences.i: and before that he had taken from them the use of words, and of a tongue born for terrible false oaths:
sentences.n: Nec non is a double negative used for emphasis, “and not not”, which in practice means “and what is more”. Prius sets the loss of speech before the sending just described, so the sentence tells the two events in the reverse of the order in which they happened. Usum governs two genitives at once, verborum and linguae: the use of words, and the use of the tongue. The genitive natae ... linguae is wrapped round dira in periuria, which it governs, and in with the accusative here expresses purpose — “born for dreadful perjuries”, a tongue made for the crime rather than merely used for it. Periuria is the same word as at 91, where the perjuries were the reason for the punishment: the sentence is cut to fit the organ that committed the offence.

sentences.t: posse queri tantum rauco stridore reliquit.
sentences.l: he left them the power only to complain, with a hoarse screech.
sentences.i: all that he left them was the power to voice a grievance, in a hoarse screech.
sentences.n: The object of reliquit is the whole infinitive phrase posse queri, an infinitive used as a noun — “the being able to complain” — which English has to turn into a noun, “the power to complain”. Tantum, “only”, limits it: they keep that and nothing else. Queri is deponent, passive in form and active in meaning, “to complain, to make a lament”, and it is a word for grievance, which is exactly what a screech cannot carry. Rauco stridore is an ablative of means: stridor is the harsh grating sound of a hinge or a beast, raucus is hoarse. The line answers usum verborum, which is split across the line-end between 98 and 99 — the voice is left and the words are taken away — and closes the story that the island's name at 90 had promised.
